white-alien-gambit-main.name: Alien Gambit: f7 Attack
white-alien-gambit-main.summary: Invite ...h6, then use the knight sacrifice on f7 only when development and forcing checks justify the material investment.

black-alien-gambit-defense.name: Alien Gambit: Calm Defense
black-alien-gambit-defense.summary: Do not help the attack with ...h6. Develop, cover f7, and use ...c5 or ...e6 to challenge White’s center.

black-caro-kann-main.summary: Use the c6-d5 structure to contest the center while developing the light-square bishop actively.

guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:idea:8.title: create a hook
guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:idea:8.text: Ng5 makes ...h6 uncomfortable and prepares the f7 idea.

guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:idea:10.title: force the king
guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:idea:10.text: Nxf7 is the signature sacrifice: play forcing moves while Black is uncoordinated.

guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:mistake.title: do not rush
guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:mistake.text: If Black does not weaken f7, develop or reroute the knight instead of sacrificing automatically.

guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:mistake.title: calculate checks
guidance:white-alien-gambit-main:mistake.text: After Nxf7, every attacking move must be checked for a real continuation.

guidance:black-alien-gambit-defense:idea.title: avoid the hook
guidance:black-alien-gambit-defense:idea.text: Nbd7 develops and protects key squares without giving White the desired ...h6 tempo.

guidance:black-alien-gambit-defense:mist.title: do not chase blindly
guidance:black-alien-gambit-defense:mist.text: ...h6 invites Nxf7 and gives White the practical attack.

guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:0.title: contest center
guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:0.text: Claim central space so both bishops and the queen knight can develop naturally.

guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:2.title: develop
guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:2.text: The knight supports e4, watches d5, and keeps the f-pawn free for active play.

guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:4.title: create threat
guidance:white-vienna-main:idea:4.text: The f-pawn challenges Black before the position settles into quiet symmetry.

guidance:white-vienna-main:mistake:2.title: avoid drift
guidance:white-vienna-main:mistake:2.text: Early queen moves usually give Black easy developing tempi.

guidance:white-vienna-main:mistake:4.title: prepare breaks
guidance:white-vienna-main:mistake:4.text: Pushing without enough piece support can leave e4 and the king exposed.

guidance:white-london-solid:idea:0.title: contest center
guidance:white-london-solid:idea:0.text: The d-pawn takes space and prepares a reliable development pattern.

guidance:white-london-solid:idea:2.title: improve worst piece
guidance:white-london-solid:idea:2.text: The bishop leaves the pawn chain before e3 closes its natural diagonal.

guidance:white-london-solid:idea:4.title: build structure
guidance:white-london-solid:idea:4.text: The e-pawn supports d4 and gives the king a calm route to safety.

guidance:white-london-solid:mistake:2.title: piece quality
guidance:white-london-solid:mistake:2.text: Locking the bishop inside the chain makes later plans feel cramped.

guidance:white-london-solid:mistake:6.title: finish development
guidance:white-london-solid:mistake:6.text: Starting flank attacks before the kingside pieces are out weakens the setup.

guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:1.title: contest center
guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:1.text: The c-pawn fights d4 from the side and keeps Black from mirroring White.

guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:3.title: stabilize center
guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:3.text: The d-pawn supports c5 and prepares development without surrendering central squares.

guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:5.title: open file
guidance:black-sicilian-basic:idea:5.text: Trading on d4 gives Black a half-open c-file for later rook activity.

guidance:black-sicilian-basic:mistake:3.title: king safety
guidance:black-sicilian-basic:mistake:3.text: Chasing pawns before developing can leave Black behind in a sharp open game.

guidance:black-sicilian-basic:mistake:5.title: file play
guidance:black-sicilian-basic:mistake:5.text: Recapturing too slowly lets White keep a space edge without pressure.

guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:1.title: prepare break
guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:1.text: The c-pawn supports d5 so Black can challenge the center with a firm base.

guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:5.title: exchange
guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:5.text: Trading in the center clarifies the structure and gives Black simple development.

guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:7.title: develop outside chain
guidance:black-caro-kann-main:idea:7.text: The bishop becomes active before e6 builds the compact pawn shell.

guidance:black-caro-kann-main:mistake:5.title: timing
guidance:black-caro-kann-main:mistake:5.text: Ignoring the central tension can let White choose a more comfortable structure.

guidance:black-caro-kann-main:mistake:7.title: piece quality
guidance:black-caro-kann-main:mistake:7.text: Trapping the bishop behind e6 too early reduces Black light-square control.

motif:alien-white-sacrifice-trigger.title: Black has played ...h6. Is the Alien sacrifice ready?
motif:alien-white-sacrifice-trigger.trigger: Black has played ...h6. Is the Alien sacrifice ready?
motif:alien-white-sacrifice-trigger.prerequisites: The knight has been chased to the square that attacks f7.
motif:alien-white-sacrifice-trigger.limitation: Nxf7 is the thematic practical sacrifice, but the compensation depends on continuing with forcing development.

motif:alien-black-defense-choice.title: White has played Ng5. Choose a calm defensive plan before the f7 sacrifice is enabled.
motif:alien-black-defense-choice.trigger: White has played Ng5. Choose a calm defensive plan before the f7 sacrifice is enabled.
motif:alien-black-defense-choice.prerequisites: Develop a piece and keep f7 protected without creating a target.
motif:alien-black-defense-choice.limitation: Nbd7 is a practical defensive move: it develops, supports the center, and avoids the ...h6 hook.

motif:vienna-f4-trigger.title: Black has developed naturally. Choose the move that creates the Vienna initiative.
motif:vienna-f4-trigger.trigger: Black has developed naturally. Choose the move that creates the Vienna initiative.
motif:vienna-f4-trigger.prerequisites: Challenge e5 before the position becomes quiet.
motif:vienna-f4-trigger.limitation: f4 is the thematic break, but normal development remains playable when you prefer less risk.

motif:vienna-central-capture.title: Black struck with ...d5. Resolve the center before continuing the attack.
motif:vienna-central-capture.trigger: Black struck with ...d5. Resolve the center before continuing the attack.
motif:vienna-central-capture.prerequisites: The e5 pawn is the anchor of Black center.
motif:vienna-central-capture.limitation: Opening aggression works only when forcing central replies are calculated first.

motif:caro-center-resolution.title: White has defended the center. Choose the Caro-Kann structural decision.
motif:caro-center-resolution.trigger: White has defended the center. Choose the Caro-Kann structural decision.
motif:caro-center-resolution.prerequisites: Clarify e4 before developing the bishop outside the chain.
motif:caro-center-resolution.limitation: The exchange makes the active bishop development possible; ...Nf6 is playable but belongs to a different structure.

motif:caro-bishop-development.title: Develop the light-squared bishop before building the compact pawn shell.
motif:caro-bishop-development.trigger: Develop the light-squared bishop before building the compact pawn shell.
motif:caro-bishop-development.prerequisites: Do not trap the bishop behind ...e6.
motif:caro-bishop-development.limitation: Active piece placement is what makes the Caro-Kann solid rather than passive.

deviation:white-vienna-main:1:0.guidance: Black declined 1...e5. Keep the e4 center, develop naturally, and treat the result as a new opening branch rather than a failed Vienna.

deviation:white-vienna-main:3:1.guidance: Black chose a different setup. Protect e4, finish development, and only play f4 when the center is stable.

deviation:black-caro-kann-main:2:0.guidance: White did not play d4. Continue with ...d5 when it is sound, develop the light bishop before ...e6, and avoid storing a separate branch for every quiet move.

deviation:black-caro-kann-main:4:1.guidance: White chose a different development order. Maintain the c6–d5 center and develop the light bishop actively before closing it in.

concept:vienna-f4-timing.title: Time the f-pawn break
concept:vienna-f4-timing.principle: Challenge e5 when the centre is stable
concept:vienna-f4-timing.summary: The Vienna f-pawn is a lever, not an automatic move. Use it when e4 is supported and Black has not created a forcing central problem.
concept:vienna-f4-timing.planPrompt: What must be true before f4 becomes a useful Vienna move?

planChoices.label: e4 is supported and the move challenges Black before the position settles.
planChoices.feedback: Exactly: f4 works because it questions e5 while your centre can absorb the tension.

planChoices.label: The opening is called the Vienna, so f4 should be played regardless of Black’s setup.
planChoices.feedback: Opening ideas are conditional. Check the centre and development before using the lever.

planChoices.label: You should already be ready to push every kingside pawn.
planChoices.feedback: The goal is central pressure, not a pawn race with an unsafe king.

scenarios.prompt: Black develops naturally. Choose how to create or prepare the Vienna initiative.
scenarios.change: Black attacks e4 and has not challenged the centre with ...d5.
scenarios.hint: Ask whether e5 can be challenged before Black castles.
scenarios.teachingPoint: f4 is the thematic break; Nf3 is also sound when you prefer to prepare it.
scenarios.watchFor: If Black strikes with ...d5, resolve the centre before continuing the attack.

scenarios.prompt: Black supports e5 with ...Nc6. Choose a useful continuation without forcing a memorized line.
scenarios.change: The e5 pawn has another defender, so preparation is more valuable.
scenarios.hint: Develop or challenge the centre; both can serve the same attacking plan.
scenarios.teachingPoint: A plan can survive different move orders: f4, Nf3, and Bc4 all contribute to central pressure and development.
scenarios.watchFor: Do not allow a quick ...d5 to hit an unsupported centre.

concept:vienna-centre-first.title: Resolve the centre first
concept:vienna-centre-first.summary: When Black plays ...d5, the position becomes concrete. Decide the central tension before adding more attackers.
concept:vienna-centre-first.planPrompt: Black challenges your Vienna centre with ...d5. What takes priority?

planChoices.label: Calculate the central captures and decide what happens to e4 and e5.
planChoices.feedback: Right: a forcing central break outranks a slow attacking move.

planChoices.label: Ignore the centre and bring the queen toward the kingside.
planChoices.feedback: The attack has no foundation if Black can remove or win the central pawns.

planChoices.label: Start another pawn push on the wing.
planChoices.feedback: First respond where the position has changed: in the centre.

scenarios.prompt: Black has played the forcing central break. Choose your response.
scenarios.change: The e5 pawn is now the anchor of Black’s centre and your f-pawn is already committed.
scenarios.hint: Look at the pawn that holds Black’s centre together.
scenarios.teachingPoint: fxe5 resolves the tension and keeps the initiative concrete; d3 is quieter but defensible.
scenarios.watchFor: After exchanges, develop quickly instead of trying to recreate the original attack.

scenarios.prompt: Black develops instead of breaking immediately. Improve the position while keeping the central plan alive.
scenarios.change: There is no forcing contact yet, but ...d5 remains Black’s thematic reply.
scenarios.hint: Improve a piece and make the centre easier to defend.
scenarios.teachingPoint: Nf3 develops, protects key squares, and makes the coming central break easier to meet.
scenarios.watchFor: Recalculate if ...d5 arrives; do not continue on autopilot.

concept:vienna-convert-initiative.title: Convert initiative into development
concept:vienna-convert-initiative.summary: Once the centre changes, use the open lines by developing and castling rather than moving the same attackers repeatedly.
concept:vienna-convert-initiative.planPrompt: After the Vienna centre opens, how should you preserve the initiative?

planChoices.label: Develop a new piece, secure the king, and only then use the open lines.
planChoices.feedback: Yes: development turns temporary activity into a sustainable attack.

planChoices.label: Move the queen repeatedly to search for an immediate threat.
planChoices.feedback: Queen moves often give Black free developing tempi.

planChoices.label: Sacrifice material simply because the position is open.
planChoices.feedback: Open lines help developed pieces; they do not justify an unsupported sacrifice.

scenarios.prompt: Black’s knight centralizes. Find a move that develops while questioning it.
scenarios.change: The centre has opened and Black’s knight occupies e4.
scenarios.hint: Bring a new piece into play with tempo.
scenarios.teachingPoint: Nf3 develops and attacks the centralized knight; the move serves both time and coordination.
scenarios.watchFor: Do not chase the knight with pawns if that further weakens your king.

scenarios.prompt: Black prepares to castle. Choose a move that makes your initiative sustainable.
scenarios.change: Black is one move from king safety, so undeveloped pieces must join now.
scenarios.hint: Develop the bishop or use the centre to open it.
scenarios.teachingPoint: Be2 or Bc4 prepares castling and adds a real piece to the position; d4 is a principled central alternative.
scenarios.watchFor: If the attack disappears, finish development instead of manufacturing tactics.

concept:caro-resolve-centre.title: Choose the Caro-Kann structure
concept:caro-resolve-centre.principle: Clarify the centre with a purpose
concept:caro-resolve-centre.summary: The central exchange is valuable because it frees the light-squared bishop before ...e6 builds the pawn shell.
concept:caro-resolve-centre.planPrompt: Why does Black often resolve the e4–d5 tension in the Classical Caro-Kann?

planChoices.label: It clarifies the structure and creates time to develop the light bishop actively.
planChoices.feedback: Exactly: the exchange and bishop development are one connected plan.

planChoices.label: Exchanges are always good for Black regardless of the resulting pieces.
planChoices.feedback: The point is the resulting structure and bishop activity, not exchanging for its own sake.

planChoices.label: Black expects to keep the e4 pawn permanently.
planChoices.feedback: White normally recaptures; Black gains a clear development scheme, not a free pawn.

scenarios.prompt: White reinforces e4. Choose the structural decision that enables active development.
scenarios.change: White can no longer be pressured by a simple central attack; the tension should be resolved deliberately.
scenarios.hint: Ask how the light bishop will get outside the pawn chain.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...dxe4 clears the diagonal for ...Bf5; ...Nf6 is playable but can lead to a different structure.
scenarios.watchFor: After White recaptures, develop the bishop before playing ...e6.

scenarios.prompt: White advances and closes the centre. Choose active development for the new structure.
scenarios.change: The centre is now a pawn chain, so the plan changes from exchange to attacking its base.
scenarios.hint: Develop the light bishop before ...e6 and then challenge d4.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...Bf5 preserves the Caro-Kann’s good bishop and prepares pressure on the pawn chain.
scenarios.watchFor: Prepare ...c5 rather than defending passively behind the chain.

concept:caro-bishop-first.title: Free the good bishop
concept:caro-bishop-first.summary: The Caro-Kann is solid because the light bishop becomes active before the compact structure is completed.
concept:caro-bishop-first.planPrompt: Which piece-placement rule keeps the Classical Caro-Kann active?

planChoices.label: Develop the light bishop before closing its diagonal with ...e6.
planChoices.feedback: Correct: this is the structural detail that prevents a passive position.

planChoices.label: Play ...e6 immediately and solve the bishop later.
planChoices.feedback: That locks the bishop behind its own pawns without gaining anything concrete.

planChoices.label: Move the queen early so the bishop can remain at home.
planChoices.feedback: The queen does not solve the bishop’s diagonal or improve minor-piece quality.

scenarios.prompt: White recaptures in the centre. Develop the piece that defines Black’s setup.
scenarios.change: The e4 pawn is gone and the light bishop has a clear diagonal.
scenarios.hint: Use the diagonal before a pawn blocks it.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...Bf5 is the active Caro-Kann move; ...Nf6 is sound but postpones the key structural task.
scenarios.watchFor: Meet h4 with a retreat that preserves the bishop rather than trapping it.

scenarios.prompt: White questions the active bishop. Preserve it without abandoning the structure.
scenarios.change: The bishop is being challenged, but it remains the piece you worked to activate.
scenarios.hint: Keep the bishop safe and useful; material is not under threat elsewhere.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...Bg6 keeps the bishop active and supports the compact setup that follows.
scenarios.watchFor: If h4–h5 arrives, choose the retreat before the bishop runs out of squares.

concept:caro-active-break.title: Challenge the pawn chain
concept:caro-active-break.summary: Against the Advance structure, Black must challenge d4 instead of accepting a permanent space disadvantage.
concept:caro-active-break.planPrompt: What turns the Caro-Kann from solid-but-passive into active counterplay?

planChoices.label: Prepare ...c5 to attack the base of White’s pawn chain.
planChoices.feedback: Right: the break questions d4 and opens useful lines for Black’s pieces.

planChoices.label: Keep every pawn fixed and wait for White to attack.
planChoices.feedback: Without a break, White keeps the space advantage for free.

planChoices.label: Push kingside pawns before developing.
planChoices.feedback: The relevant target is the central chain, and king safety still matters.

scenarios.prompt: White develops quietly. Strike at the base of the pawn chain.
scenarios.change: White is close to castling and the d4 chain is stable unless Black challenges it.
scenarios.hint: Attack d4 with the pawn that was prepared on move one.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...c5 is the thematic equalizing break; development is acceptable when it directly supports that break.
scenarios.watchFor: Do not open the centre before your king and pieces can use the new lines.

scenarios.prompt: White reinforces d4 after ...c5. Increase pressure with development.
scenarios.change: The base is defended, so Black needs another attacker rather than a premature exchange.
scenarios.hint: Develop toward d4 or attack it with the queen.
scenarios.teachingPoint: ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 add pressure while improving Black’s pieces; the break is a plan, not a one-move trick.
scenarios.watchFor: Check b2 tactics, but do not pawn-hunt while your king remains in the centre.

lesson:vienna-development.title: Vienna: turn initiative into a plan

endgame.title: Vienna: when an initiative becomes a king ending
endgame.introduction: A separate, authored training example. The advanced e5 pawn, missing f-pawn, and doubled c-pawns recall features of the Vienna lesson, but this is not its next position. Follow a legal illustrative sequence to see what survives a queen and rook exchange. No forced win is implied.

steps.title: What survives a queen exchange?
steps.prompt: Investigate a queen trade and predict how the recapture changes the pawn structure and files.
steps.hint: Exchange on e6. The f7 pawn can recapture.

choices.label: The recapture leaves e5 as a passed pawn with a clear route forward.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: The e5 space advantage remains, but the attack becomes a structural question.
choices.feedback: The pawns keep their strengths and weaknesses when queens leave.

choices.label: The recapturing pawn keeps the f-file closed to the rooks.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: Qxe6 fxe6 removes the queens and opens the f-file. Your e5 pawn still restricts squares, while the doubled c-pawns remain. Judge exchanges using the resulting position.

steps.title: Inspect the pawn ending
steps.prompt: Investigate the available rook exchange. What must replace your former attacking plan in the resulting position?
steps.hint: The f-file is now clear between the rooks.

choices.label: Continue the same rook attack after exchanging the last rooks.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: Activate the king and defend pawn weaknesses before pushing pawns.
choices.feedback: With major pieces gone, king routes and pawn targets matter.

choices.label: Push e6 immediately because the opponent’s king cannot recapture.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: Rxf8+ Kxf8 reaches a king-and-pawn ending. This is a position to evaluate before committing to the trade, not proof that simplifying is best.

steps.title: Replace the attacking pieces with your king
steps.prompt: Take a first step toward the centre while keeping your pawn structure intact.
steps.hint: Bring the king toward e3 without committing a pawn.

choices.label: Win the e6 pawn immediately with this single king move.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: Bring the king toward e3 to support the centre and inspect entry squares.
choices.feedback: The king becomes a working piece in the ending.

choices.label: Force Black’s king to stay on f8 for the rest of the ending.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: Kf2 Ke7 develops both kings. Before advancing e5 or a queenside pawn, examine the opposing king’s route and which pawns need protection. Other king moves require their own calculation.

openingExplanations: Develop while keeping the f-pawn free.
Challenge e5; this makes king safety more urgent.
Resolve the pawn contact before making another attacking move.
Black captures e4 and centralizes the knight.
Develop a defender and improve coordination.
Black prepares to castle; White must complete development too.
lesson:vienna-development.introduction: The pawn exchange has changed the centre. Your e5 pawn gives space, but the king and bishop still need attention. Build a position that can support an attack.
lesson:vienna-development.takeaway: Use the initiative to develop and secure the king. When a forcing exchange arrives, resolve it before continuing your plan.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful feature to recognize here?
questions.hint: Compare the e5 pawn, the missing f-pawn, and the undeveloped bishop.

choices.label: White should recover the e4 pawn before making a developing move.
choices.feedback: The bishop and king still need attention before the open lines become an asset.

choices.label: White should advance e5 again before Black can blockade it.
choices.feedback: The central exchange and Black knight on e4 make concrete moves important.

choices.label: White has central space, but the open lines also make king safety urgent.
choices.feedback: The e5 pawn restricts Black, while the missing f-pawn makes a king left on e1 more vulnerable.

questions.prompt: Which plan makes your initiative sustainable?
questions.hint: Bring another piece into play and connect the rooks.

choices.label: Prepare g4 to dislodge the central knight before developing.
choices.feedback: More pawn moves do not solve the undeveloped bishop or exposed king.

choices.label: Bring the queen to e2 and postpone castling to defend e5.
choices.feedback: Queen moves give Black time while your own pieces remain uncoordinated.

choices.label: Develop the bishop, castle, then support the centre with d4.
choices.feedback: This connects king safety, development, and a defended central presence.

lesson:vienna-development.transferExplanation: Rewind to just after Be2. Instead of developing with ...Nc6, Black exchanges on c3 immediately. Respond to the capture before returning to king safety.

develop.prompt: Prepare king safety by developing the remaining kingside piece.
develop.change: Black has just developed the bishop to e7.
develop.hint: Move the bishop off f1 so castling becomes possible.

answers.feedback: Be2 clears f1. Black develops with ...Nc6; now secure the king.

comparisons.Bc4: Bc4 develops toward f7, but c4 is attacked by the d5 pawn. Calculate …dxc4 before treating this as interchangeable with Be2.
comparisons.Be2: Be2 clears f1 for castling without placing the bishop on a square attacked by d5.
comparisons.d4: d4 supports e5 and opens the c1 bishop. The f1 bishop and king still need attention; compare Black’s forcing replies.

castle.prompt: Make the king safe before opening the centre further.
castle.change: Black has developed another piece; your castling path is clear.
castle.hint: Both squares between king and rook are empty.

answers.feedback: Castling connects king safety to rook activity. Black also castles.

centre.prompt: Support your advanced e5 pawn and release the queenside bishop.
centre.change: Both kings are safe. You can now reinforce the centre.
centre.hint: Use the d-pawn to support e5.

answers.feedback: d4 supports e5, but ...Nxc3 is a forcing interruption. Deal with it before developing again.

recapture.prompt: Black captured your knight. Remove the attacker before it takes another piece.
recapture.change: The black knight on c3 attacks the bishop on e2 with check available.
recapture.hint: Your b-pawn can capture the knight on c3.

mistakes.Qd3: After Qd3, ...Nxe2+ wins your bishop with check. Recapture the knight first.

answers.feedback: bxc3 restores material balance and reinforces d4. Ignoring the knight permits ...Nxe2+.

transfer-recapture.prompt: The exchange happened before d4. Recapture while opening the c1 bishop.
transfer-recapture.change: The d-pawn is still on d2, so it can now take on c3.
transfer-recapture.hint: Use the d-pawn rather than copying the earlier b-pawn recapture.

answers.feedback: dxc3 restores material and opens the bishop diagonal. The different timing changed the useful recapture.

transfer-castle.prompt: With the forcing capture resolved, return to the original priority.
transfer-castle.change: Black has developed with ...Nc6. Your king is still on e1.

answers.feedback: The exact pawn structure changed, but developing and securing the king remain useful priorities.

lesson:caro-active.title: Caro-Kann: stay solid and active

endgame.title: Caro-Kann: from the central break to an active rook
endgame.introduction: A separate, authored training position with reduced material. This is not the next position in your opening line or a historical game. White’s e-pawn is gone and the c-pawn has advanced to c3. It isolates the same …c5 idea: challenge d4, inspect the new pawn structure, then decide what the exchanges give your rook. Replay every move below. The continuation is illustrative, not forced.

steps.title: Prepare the structural change
steps.prompt: Black to move. Find a pawn move that challenges White’s central support.
steps.hint: Which pawn can attack d4 without moving your e6 pawn?

choices.label: Keep c6 fixed and organize a kingside pawn advance.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: Challenge d4 and open possibilities on the c-file.
choices.feedback: The c-pawn is the lever against d4.

choices.label: Trade the e6 pawn first to make d5 an outpost.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: …c5 attacks d4. In this example White plays b3, leaving the central tension unresolved. White could choose a different response; assess that before following the plan.

steps.title: Calculate the central exchange
steps.prompt: White has played b3. Resolve the central contact and anticipate the recapture.
steps.hint: Capture the d4 pawn. Which white pawn can recapture?

choices.label: After cxd4, White retains pawns on both c3 and d4.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: After cxd4, d4 is isolated; the c-file has no pawns.
choices.feedback: White has no c- or e-pawn beside the new d4 pawn.

choices.label: After cxd4, Black has a half-open c-file against c3.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: …cxd4 cxd4 leaves an isolated d-pawn. The pawn offers space, but it must be defended by pieces. The open c-file is a route for your rook, not a guarantee of a winning position.

steps.title: Choose an exchange deliberately
steps.prompt: The queens face each other. Investigate a simplification that keeps your rook active. Which structural feature survives?
steps.hint: Exchange on d3; look at the file your own rook can use afterwards.

choices.label: Remove the d4 target because the white rook’s recapture repairs the pawn structure.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: Reduce queen threats while retaining the open c-file and d4 target.
choices.feedback: The isolated pawn stays on d4 and both rooks remain.

choices.label: Trade queens to prevent White from defending d4 with an active rook.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: …Qxd3 Rxd3 is a rook ending. Compare the active white rook with your own access to c1 before choosing this trade in a real game. This exercise does not claim that every queen trade favors Black.

steps.title: Turn the open file into activity
steps.prompt: Use the open file with a forcing move. Predict how White can answer the check.
steps.hint: Look for a rook check on White’s back rank. The h2 square is available.

choices.label: Use a rook check that immediately wins White’s rook on d3.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: Use a check to enter the back rank before attacking the second rank.
choices.feedback: The check gains access; it does not itself win material.

choices.label: Exchange rooks immediately and race the kingside pawns.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: …Rc1+ Kh2 activates the rook. The next question is which second-rank targets are actually vulnerable. White’s rook remains active, so keep checking threats.

steps.title: Transfer: activity still needs calculation
steps.prompt: The defender has changed. Which second-rank pawn can Black safely take?
steps.transferContext: New transfer exercise: the white rook is on f1, defending f2, while Black’s rook has reached c2. This is a separate training position. Apply the open-file idea without copying a capture blindly.
steps.hint: Compare a2 with f2. Trace the white rook’s line of defence.

choices.label: f2 can be taken with check before White can recapture.
choices.feedback: That may describe another position. Check the pawn contacts and protected squares on this board.

choices.label: a2 is undefended; f2 is protected by the rook on f1.
choices.feedback: Activity creates choices; counting defenders determines the capture.

choices.label: a2 is defended along the first rank by the rook on f1.
choices.feedback: Check what remains after the exchange rather than assuming that simplification is automatically helpful.

steps.explanation: …Rxa2 wins the undefended pawn. …Rxf2? would allow Rxf2, losing your rook for a pawn. The opening’s open-file plan becomes an endgame calculation about defenders.

openingExplanations: Develop the bishop before closing its diagonal with ...e6.
Retreat while keeping the bishop outside the pawn chain.
White threatens h5 to chase the bishop.
Give the bishop a retreat on h7.
lesson:caro-active.introduction: Your light-squared bishop is active, but White is gaining space with the h-pawn. Respond to that pressure, finish development, and prepare to challenge d4.
lesson:caro-active.takeaway: Protect useful piece activity, exchange an attacking bishop when appropriate, then use development to support central counterplay.

questions.hint: Where is the light-squared bishop compared with your e-pawn?

choices.label: The centre is fixed, so the bishop can stay on g6 without a retreat.
choices.feedback: Your e-pawn is still on e7 and the bishop is already on g6.

choices.label: The bishop exchange should be postponed until after Black castles.
choices.feedback: h5 attacks the bishop directly; concrete threats interrupt long-term plans.

choices.label: The light bishop is outside the pawn shell, but White can chase it with h5.
choices.feedback: Its active placement is valuable, and ...h6 has prepared h7 as a retreat.

questions.prompt: How should Black connect defence to counterplay?
questions.hint: Solve the bishop threat, then ask what development prepares.

choices.label: Prepare a queenside pawn expansion before committing the knights.
choices.feedback: Pawn moves alone leave your king and minor pieces unready for central play.

choices.label: Keep the c-pawn on c6 and concentrate on defending d5.
choices.feedback: The solid structure should support an active central break.

choices.label: Keep the bishop safe, finish development, and challenge d4 with ...c5.
choices.feedback: Each step prepares the next: piece safety, coordination, king safety, then central play.

lesson:caro-active.transferExplanation: Rewind to the model position after ...h6. White plays Bd3 instead of h5. You can exchange the bishop directly, without copying the retreat to h7.

bishop-retreat.prompt: White attacks your bishop. Use the retreat you prepared.
bishop-retreat.change: h5 has attacked the bishop on g6.
bishop-retreat.hint: The h7 square is available because your pawn moved to h6.

answers.feedback: Bh7 preserves the bishop. White develops, so now build your central shell.

shell.prompt: Support the centre and open the dark-squared bishop.
shell.change: Your light bishop is safely outside the pawn chain.

answers.feedback: ...e6 supports d5 and releases f8. White now offers a bishop exchange.

exchange.prompt: Resolve the bishop contact while preserving kingside castling.
exchange.change: Bd3 attacks your bishop along d3–h7.
exchange.hint: Exchange on d3 before White captures on h7.

mistakes.a6: This ignores the bishop contact. Bxh7 followed by ...Rxh7 would give up kingside castling. Exchange on d3 first in this plan.

answers.feedback: ...Bxd3 removes the attacking bishop. After a waiting move, Bxh7 followed by ...Rxh7 would move the rook and forfeit kingside castling.

queen-knight.prompt: Develop a knight to support future central play.
queen-knight.change: The bishops have been exchanged and White prepares king safety.
queen-knight.hint: Bring the b8 knight to d7.

answers.feedback: ...Nd7 develops without obstructing the c-pawn break.

king-knight.prompt: Develop the remaining knight toward the centre.
king-knight.change: White has castled and can soon bring a rook to the centre.
king-knight.hint: Move the g8 knight, keeping the d7 knight in support.

answers.feedback: ...Ngf6 brings the last knight into play.

king-bishop.prompt: Clear the last square needed for castling.
king-bishop.change: White has placed a rook on e1.

answers.feedback: ...Be7 finishes the preparation for king safety.

safe-king.prompt: Secure the king before challenging the centre.
safe-king.change: White has completed development and is bringing pressure to the d-file.
safe-king.hint: The kingside castling route is clear.

answers.feedback: Your king is safe. The next step is active central counterplay.

break.prompt: Challenge the base of White’s central space.
break.change: Both sides have developed; your pieces can support the pawn break.

answers.feedback: ...c5 challenges d4. Reassess the captures instead of following a fixed sequence after the break.

transfer-exchange.prompt: White developed the bishop instead of chasing yours. Resolve this new contact.
transfer-exchange.change: The bishop on d3 now faces your bishop on g6.
transfer-exchange.hint: You can exchange immediately on d3.

answers.feedback: You do not need ...Bh7: White chose a different move, so exchange directly.

transfer-shell.prompt: Return to the development plan after the exchange.
transfer-shell.change: White recaptured with the queen; your light bishop no longer needs a retreat.
transfer-shell.hint: Open the f8 bishop and support the centre.

answers.feedback: ...e6 returns to the same development goal through a different move order.

transfer-knight.prompt: Prepare active central play with a developing move.
transfer-knight.change: White has developed the kingside knight.
transfer-knight.hint: Bring the b8 knight into play without blocking the c-pawn.

answers.feedback: ...Nd7 supports the central plan. Finish development and check the timing of ...c5 during practical play.

continuation.title: Caro-Kann: follow the centre into a rook ending
continuation.introduction: An original illustrative continuation of the main lesson after …c5, not a historical game or a forced sequence. We return to that main-line position even if you last played the alternate bishop exchange. White chooses c3 and later cxd4 so we can follow the isolated pawn. Other replies change the plan. Every position below is reached by the replayed moves.

steps.title: Resolve or maintain the central tension
steps.prompt: White has reinforced d4 with c3. Choose how to handle the contact between c5 and d4.
steps.hint: Compare exchanging on d4 with bringing the a8 rook to the c-file before exchanging.
steps.takeaway: An exchange clarifies the structure; a rook move can increase pressure while keeping the tension.

bridge.note: White supports d4 with a pawn; a later c-pawn recapture would leave d4 isolated.

main.note: White chooses the pawn recapture: d4 is isolated and the c-file opens. Nxd4 would produce a different structure.

choices.label: Clarify the pawn structure by exchanging on d4.
choices.feedback: After …cxd4 cxd4, White has no c- or e-pawn beside d4. White gains open lines as well as a pawn to defend.

choices.label: Place the rook on the c-file and keep the pawn contact.
choices.feedback: …Rc8 brings a rook behind the c-pawn. It preserves the choice of when to exchange.

choices.label: Force an isolated pawn regardless of White’s recapture.
choices.feedback: White can also recapture Nxd4. Isolation follows the example’s cxd4, not every legal reply.

candidates.explanation: Exchange now, then inspect White’s recapture.

replies.explanation: cxd4 keeps a pawn on d4 but leaves it isolated.
Nxd4 is also sound. White avoids the isolated pawn; reassess the piece activity instead of copying the example’s pawn plan.

candidates.explanation: Prepare pressure before deciding whether to exchange. The c-pawn still blocks the file.

replies.explanation: Qe2 moves the queen away from d3 and supports central play. The tension remains.

steps.title: Use the square in front of the isolated pawn
steps.prompt: White’s pawn is isolated on d4. Choose a piece improvement that addresses this structure.
steps.hint: Compare placing the f6 knight on d5 with using the newly opened c-file.
steps.takeaway: The isolated pawn provides space, but d5 is a blockading square and the c-file offers rook activity.

main.note: The f6 knight blockades d4 and attacks the bishop on f4.
A weaker illustrative reply: White offers the bishop. Bc1 is the stronger retreat; …f6 would test Be5 more severely than our simplifying exchange.

choices.label: Occupy d5 to restrict the pawn and gain a tempo on the bishop.
choices.feedback: …Nd5 blocks d4’s advance and attacks f4. White must account for the bishop contact.

choices.label: Use the open c-file while leaving the knight on f6.
choices.feedback: …Rc8 activates the a8 rook without immediately blockading d4.

choices.label: Win d4 immediately because isolated pawns cannot be defended.
choices.feedback: The d4 pawn is defended by pieces. Isolation creates a responsibility, not a forced win.

candidates.explanation: Occupy the square in front of d4 and attack f4.

replies.explanation: Bc1 retreats the attacked bishop and preserves it. This is stronger defence than the example’s Be5.

Be5 is the illustrative reply, but weaker defence: …f6 attacks the bishop and creates concrete problems. Predict Bc1 when testing Black against stronger resistance. The example deliberately simplifies with …Nxe5 instead.

candidates.explanation: Use the open file rather than immediately blockading the pawn.

replies.explanation: Ne5 centralises White’s knight. Black must calculate the exchanges.

steps.title: Challenge the central knight
steps.prompt: A pair of minor pieces has been exchanged. White now has a knight on e5. Choose how to improve your position.
steps.hint: The bishop can challenge e5 from d6, or the rook can occupy the open file.
steps.takeaway: Piece activity determines whether a structural target is useful. Consider what a capture does to the pawns.

bridge.note: The d7 knight captures the offered bishop. We illustrate a structural exchange here; …f6 is the more testing response to Be5.
White’s f3 knight recaptures and occupies e5.

main.note: The bishop challenges e5. This illustrates a plan; it is not the engine’s unique preference.
White activates the queen, retaining the option to recapture on e5 with the d-pawn.

choices.label: Challenge e5 and consider how a d-pawn recapture changes the centre.
choices.feedback: …Bd6 attacks the knight. After a later …Bxe5 dxe5, the isolated pawn changes files.

choices.label: Activate the rook on c8 without deciding the bishop exchange yet.
choices.feedback: …Rc8 occupies the open file and retains the bishop. Keeping the bishop is a real alternative.

choices.label: Trade the bishop because bishops are always worse than knights.
choices.feedback: The exchange depends on activity and the resulting structure, not a universal piece ranking.

candidates.explanation: Confront e5 and make a structural exchange possible.

replies.explanation: Qf3 brings the queen into play. White can answer …Bxe5 with dxe5.

candidates.explanation: Rook activity can come first; this keeps the bishop and central tension.

replies.explanation: Ne4 brings White’s other knight into play. Black must still choose how to handle e5.

steps.title: Choose what the exchange gives up
steps.prompt: Compare exchanging the bishop for the e5 knight with keeping the bishop and improving a rook.
steps.hint: After …Bxe5, trace the d4 pawn’s recapture and inspect the newly opened d-file.
steps.takeaway: Removing the knight gives White an advanced e-pawn and opens the d-file. Simplification has a cost.

main.note: Black exchanges the bishop for the central knight.
The isolated d-pawn becomes an isolated e-pawn. The d-file opens; e5 gains space but needs defence.

choices.label: Remove the central knight while accepting an advanced white e-pawn.
choices.feedback: …Bxe5 dxe5 gives up the bishop. Account for White’s space and the open d-file.

choices.label: Keep the bishop and activate the rook before committing to a trade.
choices.feedback: …Rc8 retains more pieces and uses the open c-file. It postpones the structural decision.

choices.label: Repair White’s structure by connecting d4 to a neighbouring pawn.
choices.feedback: dxe5 changes the pawn’s file but does not give it an adjacent friendly pawn. It remains isolated.

candidates.explanation: A playable illustrative exchange, not a claim that trading the bishop is best.

replies.explanation: dxe5 restores material balance and places a white pawn on e5.

candidates.explanation: Keep the bishop and increase rook activity, preserving more tension.

replies.explanation: Ne4 develops a second active knight. The bishop and central knight can remain on the board.

steps.title: Offer a queen trade with the ending in view
steps.prompt: Replay the intervening exchanges. Queens, one rook each and pawns remain. Choose a queen move with a concrete plan.
steps.hint: Compare offering a supported exchange on c6 with keeping queens and using e7.
steps.takeaway: The queen exchange reduces king threats but leaves an isolated c-pawn. Rook activity matters alongside that weakness.

bridge.note: Black targets e5 with the queen.
White centralises the knight and attacks the queen.
The queen captures the advanced pawn and leaves g5.
White challenges the knight on d5.
The queen retreats along the diagonal.
White exchanges the final pair of knights.
White’s d1 rook captures that pawn on the open d-file.
The a8 rook crosses to the open e-file.
White’s e1 rook exchanges that rook.
Black’s f8 rook recaptures; one rook remains per side.
White returns the remaining rook to d1. The queens can meet along f3–c6.

main.note: Offer a queen trade on a square protected by b7.
White accepts. Black must recapture before continuing the rook plan.

choices.label: Offer a protected queen exchange, accepting an isolated c-pawn.
choices.feedback: After …Qc6 Qxc6 bxc6, the b-pawn becomes an isolated c-pawn. Queens disappear, but pawn weaknesses do not.

choices.label: Keep queens and seek active queen play from e7.
choices.feedback: …Qe7 retains queen threats and leaves the b-pawn on its original file. The ending is optional.

choices.label: Force a winning pawn ending by exchanging the queens.
choices.feedback: Both rooks remain after the queen exchange. This rook ending is not a forced win.

candidates.explanation: A supported offer: b7 can recapture on c6. Check that defence before trading queens.

replies.explanation: Qxc6 accepts the trade. …bxc6 reaches the rook ending.

candidates.explanation: Keep queens and coordinate on the e-file, rather than simplifying now.

replies.explanation: b3 secures the queenside while leaving the queen trade undecided.

steps.title: Make the rook active in the resulting ending
steps.prompt: Queens and minor pieces have gone. Black has an isolated c-pawn. Find an active rook move and anticipate White’s counterplay.
steps.hint: Compare entering the second rank with a rook lift to e5. Check White’s back-rank checks in both lines.
steps.takeaway: The c-pawn needs attention, but active rooks create threats for both sides. Keep checking the opponent’s reply.

bridge.note: The b7 pawn recaptures the queen. This same game has now reached a rook ending.
White supports h5 and creates room for the king.

main.note: Black enters the second rank and attacks a2 and b2.
White counters with a back-rank check. Black must answer it; the example does not end in a claimed win.

choices.label: Enter the second rank to create pawn threats while anticipating checks.
choices.feedback: …Re2 attacks a2 and b2. White can check on d8, so activity does not eliminate defensive duties.

choices.label: Lift the rook to e5 for lateral activity and pressure on h5.
choices.feedback: …Re5 provides lateral activity and attacks h5. White can still check on d8.

choices.label: Give a check on e1 without checking whether White can capture the rook.
choices.feedback: …Re1+? allows Rxe1. White’s rook on d1 guards the checking square.

candidates.explanation: Second-rank activity creates targets; account for White’s checks.

replies.explanation: Rd8+ is active counterplay. Black can answer …Kh7; this illustration does not establish a win.

candidates.explanation: A rook lift is another active plan, keeping lateral access to the kingside.

replies.explanation: White keeps the rook active with check. Consider …Kh7 before taking a pawn.

candidates.explanation: …Re1+ loses the rook to Rxe1. White’s rook guards the checking square.

replies.explanation: Rxe1 captures the checking rook. Check the defender on d1 before choosing a rook check.
